Communica- tion between deaf and normal people is restricted by the inability of current technology to automatically create flexible Bangla Sign Language (BdSL) animations from Bangla text or voice. This work introduces a revolutionary computer graphics-based system that takes voice or text input in Bangla and uses it to create BdSL animations. The system uses a HamNoSys to Gesture Markup Language (SiGML) conversion to dynamically translate input into gestures. With the use of 94 classes in the dataset that cover Bangla numbers, alphabets, and word motions, the model can generate any word or phrase in Bangla. Ad- ditionally, the system creates gestures for inputs that aren’t in the dataset by spelling out the letters. The system converts Bangla text into three-dimensional animated BdSL move- ments by parsing it based on Linguistic principles. According to performance evaluations, each input has a processing cost of 79.57 ms, and the average accuracy for text and voice input is 97.50% and 94.75%, respectively. The method ensures fluency and naturalness by taking into consideration crucial elements of sign language, such as hand shape, palm orientation, and non-manual messages. By reducing communication barriers between the sign and non-sign populations, this study significantly advances accessibility. While the system is very accurate (97.50% for text and 94.75% for voice input), it is currently limited in its ability to handle complicated Ban- gla phrases, idiomatic expressions, and context-specific gestures. For example, the sys- tem struggles with statements that need complex cultural or contextual interpretation, like metaphors or regional idioms. Furthermore, the absence of non-manual signals (such as facial expressions and head tilts) in the animations restricts the expressiveness of gestures, which are essential for communicating tone and emotion in sign language. These limita- tions result from the present dataset’s emphasis on conventional BdSL gestures, which do not yet account for regional variances or context-dependent signing styles. User input from native Bangla speakers emphasized the need for better handling of dialect-specific gestures and real-world conversational circumstances. Despite these limitations, the system’s Ham- NoSys-to-SiGML translation and ability to spell out unknown words show that it has the potential to be a fundamental tool in future studies. JSON: Name: bdsl_hamnosys_to_sigml_pipeline Title: A HamNoSys-to-SiGML computer-graphics pipeline with a Bangla linguistic parser for automatic generation of 3D Bangla Sign Language animations from Bangla text and speech Short Hypothesis: A pipeline that (i) converts HamNoSys transcriptions to SiGML, (ii) applies a rule-based Bangla linguistic parser, and (iii) drives a 3D avatar with the resulting SiGML will produce BdSL animations with gesture accuracy >= 95% for text input and end-to-end processing latency <= 100 ms per input on commodity hardware. Related Work: Existing approaches to automated sign-language animation fall into three categories: (1) concatenation of pre-recorded sign clips or keyframe sequences, which yields high visual fidelity for trained tokens but fails to generalize to unseen words and produces discontinuities; (2) direct SiGML/markup-driven avatar rendering, which standardizes gesture encoding but typically lacks upstream linguistic parsing and spelling fallback for out-of-vocabulary terms; and (3) data-driven neural motion synthesis (e.g., transformer or diffusion-based models) that produce fluent novel motions but require large annotated multimodal datasets, struggle with fine handshape accuracy, and incur heavy compute. Shortcomings across prior work include limited language-specific linguistics integration, sparse or nonrepresentative corpora for low-resource languages, inadequate handling of non-manual signals (facial/eye expressions), poor robustness to speech-acoustic variability and dialects, and lack of systematic latency and intelligibility evaluations for real-time applications. Abstract: We present a structured research pipeline that converts HamNoSys transcriptions into SiGML and combines that conversion with a rule-based Bangla linguistic parser to generate 3D animated Bangla Sign Language (BdSL) gestures from Bangla text and speech inputs. The pipeline formalizes mapping from linguistic tokens to HamNoSys notations, an automated HamNoSys-to-SiGML translator, a sequence generator that applies BdSL word-order rules and spelling fallback for unseen tokens, and a SiGML-driven 3D avatar renderer. The main contribution is an end-to-end, repeatable evaluation framework that measures gesture correctness, temporal consistency, and latency for BdSL generation and isolates the contribution of each pipeline stage via ablation. Expected outcomes are empirical quantification of how HamNoSys-to-SiGML conversion and linguistic parsing affect animation accuracy and responsiveness, identification of bottlenecks for real-time deployment, and a validated protocol for evaluating BdSL animation systems on low-resource languages. Experiments: Datasets: training/structured resource: 90 SiGML classes (41 words, 36 alphabets, 13 numerals) derived from HamNoSys; augmentation set: additional 6,000 HamNoSys examples adapted where applicable; speech corpus: 1,200 Bangla utterances from 90 speakers balanced across three dialect groups (Dhaka, Chittagong, Sylhet) and three age brackets; held-out test set: 1,000 inputs (500 text-only: 200 sentences, 200 words, 100 numerals; 500 speech utterances mapping to same token set). Baselines: (B1) pre-recorded sign concatenation (clip bank), (B2) direct SiGML rendering without HamNoSys intermediary or linguistic parser, (B3) neural motion synthesis (transformer/conditional VAE) trained on same set, (B4) version of proposed pipeline with spelling fallback disabled. Evaluation metrics: gesture accuracy (binary correct/incorrect per token judged by 5 independent BdSL experts; report mean accuracy and 95% CI), token-level precision/recall/F1, temporal consistency (MSE of normalized 3D joint trajectories versus expert reference), perceptual Mean Opinion Score (MOS) for naturalness and intelligibility on 5-point scale by 30 Deaf/BdSL users, end-to-end latency (ms) measured with performance.now() averaged over 1000 runs, and successful rendering rate. Experimental setup: run all systems on commodity laptop (Intel i5 11th gen, 8GB RAM, MX350 GPU); speech recognition uses same ASR module across comparisons; statistical tests: paired t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank for MOS and accuracy differences, significance alpha=0.05 with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. Ablation studies: (A1) remove HamNoSys-to-SiGML conversion and map tokens directly to SiGML, (A2) remove rule-based Bangla parser and use naive left-to-right token mapping, (A3) disable spelling fallback, (A4) add synthetic non-manual signals (head/eyebrow) to test perceptual gain. Report per-condition metrics and effect sizes. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: ASR errors (noise, accents, dialects) propagating to incorrect token selection; ambiguous or inconsistent HamNoSys annotations leading to incorrect SiGML generation; avatar kinematic limits causing unrealizable handshapes; absence or simplified modeling of non-manual signals reducing intelligibility. Data/evaluation biases: the dataset may underrepresent regional signing variants and sociolects, leading to overestimated accuracy for standard dialects; expert judgments and MOS are subjective and susceptible to rater bias. Scalability and compute: neural alternatives require orders of magnitude more annotated motion data and GPU compute; rendering complex SiGML sequences with high-fidelity hand articulation can be limited by avatar rig complexity and client hardware. Generalization limits: system tuned to BdSL token set will not generalize to other sign languages without new HamNoSys/SiGML mappings and linguistic rules; cultural or idiomatic signs that depend on context and non-manual cues may remain misinterpreted. Evaluation limits: automated metrics (trajectory MSE) do not fully capture communicative adequacy; real-world conversational turn-taking and co-articulation effects are not covered by isolated-token tests.
